highlights:
2026-08-31 23:52:06

According to Korea Investment & Securities analysts on August 1, neoclod companies reported significant GPU rental fee increases in Q2 results. CoreWeave implemented a 25% price increase across all products in July, while Nebius saw capacity auction prices 15% higher than previous highs. IREN's three-year contract rates jumped 125% versus November 2025, with five-year rates up 70%. Consequentially, data center investment payback periods have compressed from the traditional 4-5 years to under 2 years, with Nebius noting that $20 million per megawatt (MW) contracts now enable sub-two-year ROI, and IREN citing recent $25 million per MW agreements in negotiation.

Analysts attribute the surge to accelerating token consumption by enterprises. Google disclosed in Q2 that over 500 companies now consume 1 trillion-plus tokens, with 2,000+ consuming 100 billion tokens. Microsoft reported a 400% year-over-year increase in customers reaching annual token consumption of 1 trillion, driving higher profitability for AI model developers and intensifying data center pricing pressure.

results.title: GPU Cloud Pricing Statistics: September 2026 · AI Industry Reviews
highlights:
# GPU Cloud Pricing Statistics: September 2026

By Darin ten Bruggencate, Founder, AI Industry Reviews · August 29, 2026

Renting a data center GPU can cost very different amounts depending on the provider and how the capacity is sold. Teams deciding whether to rent or buy need comparable prices.

Our analysts collected 4,180 GPU-hour rental prices for 14 data center accelerators across 61 cloud providers. We gathered them between March 2 and August 29, 2026. The sample covers the three largest hyperscalers, 22 specialist GPU clouds and the major peer-to-peer marketplaces. We converted every listing to the price of a single GPU-hour so all offers can be compared directly.

In the following sections, we compare H100 prices by provider type, show when owning beats renting, and look at price spreads, trends and commitment discounts.

## H100 Pricing by Provider Category

In the table below, we compare median on-demand rates across three provider categories and express the H100 gap as a premium over the marketplace baseline.

H100 Pricing by Provider Category, September 2026

| Provider Category | H100 | H200 | B200 | H100 Premium |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Marketplace | $2.09 | $3.10 | $4.35 | Baseline |
| Specialist neocloud | $3.28 | $4.28 | $5.95 | +57% |
| Hyperscaler on-demand | $5.64 | $6.72 | $9.10 | +170% |

### Insights

- Hyperscaler H100 on-demand priced at a 170% premium to marketplace in the September sample, or $5.64 versus $2.09 per GPU-hour.
- Specialist neocloud sat between the two at $3.28, a 57% premium to marketplace.
- The same H100 costs far more from a hyperscaler than from a neocloud or a marketplace, so the provider category changes a team's bill as much as the choice of chip does.

The hyperscaler rate buys a support contract, a service level agreement, private networking into an existing cloud footprint, and compliance attestations that most specialist providers do not offer. We sorted providers by those attributes, not by company size, so two of the larger specialist fleets in the sample are in the neocloud row.

...

Owning Versus Renting Break-Even, September 2026

| GPU Model | Street Price (New) | All-In Cost ($/GPU-hr) | Median Rental | Break-Even Utilization |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| NVIDIA B200 | $46,500 | $2.68 | $6.05 | 38% |
| NVIDIA H200 | $38,000 | $2.21 | $4.31 | 44% |
| NVIDIA H100 SXM 80GB | $32,500 | $1.92 | $3.24 | 50% |
| NVIDIA A100 80GB | $9,800 | $0.84 | $1.79 | 40% |
| NVIDIA L40S | $8,400 | $0.76 | $1.48 | 44% |
| AMD MI300X | $17,500 | $1.36 | $2.87 | 40% |

### Insights

- An H100 purchase only beats median on-demand rental once the card stays busy at least 50% of the time.
- B200 breaks even at 38% utilization, the lowest threshold in the set, because rental medians remain elevated relative to street price.
- Buying GPUs pays off only for teams that keep them busy, so a company without a steady workload comes out ahead by renting.

## Price Spread by GPU Model

List price for a single provider is a narrow slice of the market. In the table below, we report the sample median on-demand rate for each model plus the 10th and 90th percentile of listings. The spread column is the 90th percentile divided by the 10th, which measures how fragmented pricing is for that card.

GPU Price Spread by Model, September 2026

| GPU Model | Median On-Demand ($/GPU-hr) | 10th Percentile | 90th Percentile | Price Spread |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| NVIDIA GB200 (per GPU) | $9.84 | $6.40 | $19.75 | 3.1x |
| NVIDIA B300 | $8.12 | $5.15 | $14.60 | 2.8x |
| NVIDIA B200 | $6.05 | $3.42 | $11.80 | 3.4x |
| NVIDIA H200 | $4.31 | $2.58 | $9.45 | 3.7x |
| NVIDIA H100 80GB | $3.24 | $1.44 | $8.90 | 6.2x |
| NVIDIA A100 80GB | $1.79 | $0.92 | $5.15 | 5.6x |
| NVIDIA L40S | $1.48 | $0.74 | $3.60 | 4.9x |
| NVIDIA V100 | $1.51 | $0.68 | $2.90 | 4.3x |
| NVIDIA RTX 5090 | $0.58 | $0.29 | $1.35 | 4.7x |
| NVIDIA RTX 4090 | $0.41 | $0.21 | $0.98 | 4.7x |
| AMD MI300X | $2.87 | $1.72 | $5.90 | 3.4x |
| Google TPU v6e (per chip) | $2.58 | $1.18 | $3.10 | 2.6x |

...

## H100 Prices by Provider Channel, Q3 2023 to Q3 2026

In the table below, we show the median quarterly on-demand H100 rate in each of the three provider channels.

H100 Prices by Provider Channel, Q3 2023 to Q3 2026

| Quarter | Hyperscaler | Specialist Neocloud | Marketplace |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Q3 2023 | $8.05 | $4.60 | $3.85 |
| Q4 2023 | $7.72 | $4.12 | $3.40 |
| Q1 2024 | $7.94 | $3.62 | $2.92 |
| Q2 2024 | $8.60 | $3.10 | $2.66 |
| Q3 2024 | $9.18 | $2.94 | $2.51 |
| Q4 2024 | $8.85 | $3.28 | $2.38 |
| Q1 2025 | $8.64 | $3.44 | $2.24 |
| Q2 2025 | $7.02 | $3.31 | $2.05 |
| Q3 2025 | $6.38 | $3.36 | $1.98 |
| Q4 2025 | $6.15 | $3.18 | $1.92 |
| Q1 2026 | $5.70 | $3.02 | $2.11 |
| Q2 2026 | $5.92 | $3.35 | $2.24 |
| Q3 2026 | $5.64 | $3.28 | $2.09 |

H100 rental prices by provider channel

In the quarterly series above, hyperscaler pricing rose through 2024 while reserved enterprise capacity stayed scarce, then fell in mid-2025 as specialist competition forced Hopper fleets to reprice. Marketplace rates fell about 50% from the third quarter of 2023 to the fourth quarter of 2025 as resellers and colocation tenants listed idle cards. We read the 2026 uptick across all three channels as the first sustained reversal in that series, and we tie it to high-bandwidth memory costs passing into rental rates.

## Commitment Discounts Versus On-Demand

In the table below, we quantify the median discount each commitment structure earns against the same provider's on-demand rate, plus the effective hourly rate a three-year commitment produces.

GPU Commitment Discounts, September 2026

| GPU Model | Spot Discount | 1-Year Reserved | 3-Year Reserved | Effective 3-Year Rate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| NVIDIA B200 | -31% | -21% | -39% | $3.69 |
| NVIDIA H200 | -38% | -24% | -42% | $2.50 |
| NVIDIA H100 80GB | -44% | -27% | -46% | $1.75 |
| NVIDIA A100 80GB | -57% | -31% | -49% | $0.91 |
| NVIDIA L40S | -63% | -34% | -51% | $0.73 |

### Insights

- Spot discounts widened with hardware age, from 31% on B200 to 63% on L40S.
- One-year reserved discounts stayed smaller than spot discounts on every model priced, so they are the weakest value for interruptible work.
- A three-year H100 commitment now prices below the median marketplace on-demand rate, a first in this series, so a team with predictable demand saves the most by committing.

results.title: CME Targets Oct. 5 Nvidia GPU Futures Launch as CFTC Tests the Benchmark | Superpower Daily
highlights:
CME Group is targeting October 5 for futures linked to Nvidia’s H100 and B200 rental prices, pending approval. It would be a new way to trade a forward price for AI compute—but not a way to reserve the chips themselves. The contracts would be cash-settled against Silicon Data benchmarks. If those benchmarks rise or fall, the contract pays out accordingly; during a shortage, though, the holder still may not get any GPUs. The proposed reference points are about $2.68 per GPU-hour for an H100 and $5.66 for a B200. The challenge is whether those numbers represent a market that is anything but uniform. Rental rates can differ by provider, location, contract length, networking, and available capacity, even for the same Nvidia model. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission, or CFTC, is taking comments through October 20—after the planned launch date—and approval is still unresolved. There are also concerns about privately produced benchmarks. Yggdrasil Financial Technologies has warned of potential conflicts, while Jessica Inskip of StockBrokers.com said the market needs genuine commercial buyers and sellers, not just managed-money trading. Earlier DRAM and bandwidth contracts struggled because standardization failed; iron ore offers a more successful index-led example. The key test is whether real compute users make this curve a trusted price signal, rather than simply another listed financial product.

...

CME’s proposed Nvidia GPU futures would create a tradable forward price for H100 and B200 compute, but not reserve physical capacity. Contracts would settle against Silicon Data benchmarks reported at $2.68 and $5.66 per GPU-hour, respectively. The key risk is whether rental prices—split by provider, location, term, networking, and availability—are consistent enough to form a credible benchmark. CME’s October 5 target precedes the CFTC’s October 20 comment deadline, leaving approval and market quality unresolved.

...

CME Group plans to launch futures tied to Nvidia H100 and B200 rental prices on October 5, pending regulatory approval. The proposed market promises a forward price for AI compute, while the CFTC is still testing whether the rental market is standardized and transparent enough to support it.

The contracts would settle against Silicon Data benchmarks, which track what companies pay to rent the two GPU types. They are financial instruments, not hardware reservations: payouts would follow benchmark-price movements, without providing chips when capacity is tight.

## A price signal, not a supply guarantee

That distinction matters because the same GPU can rent at different rates depending on the provider, location, rental term, networking and availability. The contract would track a published measure of those rates; it would not make a specific configuration available to its holder.

Reported Silicon Data benchmarks

$2.68 H100 rental benchmark

Silicon Data’s H100 benchmark was reported at about $2.68 per GPU-hour.

$5.66 B200 rental benchmark

Silicon Data’s B200 benchmark was reported at about $5.66 per GPU-hour.

...

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission is taking public comment through October 20 on whether compute-rental pricing is sufficiently standardized and transparent. That deadline falls after CME’s planned launch date, which remains subject to regulatory approval.

...

- Rental rates vary by provider, geography, term, networking and available capacity, even for the same GPU model.
- Yggdrasil Financial Technologies has warned the CFTC that privately produced benchmarks can create conflicts resembling the historical LIBOR problem.
- Jessica Inskip of StockBrokers.com said a useful futures curve requires real buyers and sellers; managed-money trading alone could make it a sentiment index.

results.title: When Compute becomes a Commodity - Rebecca Chesworth
highlights:
This market is developing at pace. What caught my eye is Ornn, founded in 2025 and backed by Andreessen Horowitz with $33 million. [3] This start-up is building financial products for compute. Its Ornn Compute Price Index (ORNNH100 Index) tracks live spot prices for GPU compute across specific hardware (NVIDIA’s H100, H200 and B200 chips). The indices are built from printed transactions rather than surveys or quotes. They are quoted on the Bloomberg Terminal, and ICE has announced cash-settled GPU-compute futures referencing them, subject to regulatory approval. [4]

...

Others are already entering the market. Silicon Data, backed by the trading house DRW, is partnering with CME Group (the world’s largest derivatives exchange) to provide a market-based forward curve for H100 spot pricing. These futures are pegged to a different set of GPU rental indices, with a confirmed launch of 5 October 2026. [7] I think that two large exchange groups building competing venues for the same underlying commodity will accelerate institutional investor interest in compute as an asset class.

...

We had a demonstration of how quickly the price can move on fears of scarcity of compute in the spot market in May 2026. Witness the price spike which resulted from a cluster of events, starting with AMD’s stronger-than-expected AI forecast (its shares surged 21% on the day) which highlighted robust GPU demand across the industry. Sentiment was heightened by CoreWeave’s strongest-ever quarter of new business and reports of companies striking deals to lock up GPU supply. Sentiment then peaked with NVIDIA’s Q1 earnings, when Jensen Huang described demand as having gone “parabolic” and Dell reporting $51.3 billion. The ORNNH100 Index captured this supply squeeze - the spot price jumped over 80% from lows of $1.75 to $3.24 on 19 May before settling into a higher range.

results.title: Spent a few hours recently with family friends who've just entered the GPU-as-a-service market. Naturally, I drew the parallel to cloud economics - years of AWS and GCP bills across two ventures … | Vaibhav Anand
highlights:
On raw H100 pricing, hyperscalers aren't cheaper - they're 2.5x to 5x more expensive than neoclouds, at every tier I checked:

→ On-demand: AWS ~$6.88/GPU-hr, Azure ~$12.29/GPU-hr, vs. ~$2.39/GPU-hr on GPU-first providers like RunPod → 3-year reserved: AWS's deepest commitment tier (~$3.10/GPU-hr) closes a lot of the gap - enough to beat most neocloud on-demand rates but neocloud reserved contracts (~$1.84/GPU-hr) still undercut it

The gap compresses with commitment. It doesn't invert.

India adds a sharper version of the same pattern. Commercial hyperscaler H100 access here runs roughly ₹210–335/GPU-hr. IndiaAI Mission-empanelled providers (Yotta, E2E Networks, Tata Communications, CtrlS) price at ₹115–150/GPU-hr before subsidy which is already below hyperscaler rates and the mission's 40% compute subsidy pushes effective rates for approved projects to ₹65–116/GPU-hr.

results.title: GPU Neocloud Infrastructure for Agent Latency | Algoramming
highlights:
GPU neocloud infrastructure provides bare-metal or lightly virtualized access to high-end accelerators, including NVIDIA H100, H200, B200, and Groq LPUs, using specialized high-throughput networking like InfiniBand. This architecture eliminates the hypervisor virtualization overhead of traditional clouds, reducing time-to-first-token latency from 300 milliseconds to under 50 milliseconds.

...

CoreWeave is the prime example of this model. Having completed its public listing on Nasdaq under the ticker CRWV, CoreWeave has built an enormous footprint. The company reported a massive 112% year-over-year revenue increase to $2.575 billion in its Q2 2026 earnings, backed by a revenue backlog of $104 billion. To fuel this growth, CoreWeave closed a $2.6 billion loan facility in August 2026 to purchase the latest hardware, including NVIDIA H200 and Blackwell B200 systems. Other capital-heavy players include Lambda Labs, which recently appointed Michel Combes as CEO, and Nebius Group.

...

CoreWeave is an accelerated compute cloud. It provides access to the full spectrum of NVIDIA hardware. This includes the Hopper generation, such as the H100 and H200, as well as the newer Blackwell generation, including the B200 and GB200 NVL72. CoreWeave is designed for flexibility. On CoreWeave, you rent raw GPU nodes, configure your own machine learning containers, choose your inference engines, such as vLLM or TensorRT-LLM, and manage your own serving stacks. This is the ideal platform if you need to run custom fine-tuned models, manage massive context windows, or run complex multi-model pipelines.

...

An NVIDIA H100 node on CoreWeave costs roughly $6.16 per GPU hour when rented on-demand, which translates to $49.28 per hour for a standard 8-GPU node. If you run a highly optimized vLLM server on that node, you can process roughly 15,000 tokens per second across all active requests. Over the course of an hour, that server can handle approximately 54 million tokens.

...

| Core Capability | Legacy Hyperscaler | Bare-Metal Neocloud (CoreWeave) | LPU Inference Cloud (GroqCloud) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Primary Billing Model | Virtual Machine Hour | Bare-Metal Node Hour | Per Million Tokens |
| Typical H100 Rate | $12.00 to $14.00 / hr | $6.16 / hr (8-GPU minimum) | N/A (Fully Managed API) |
| Orchestration Layer | ECS, AKS, GKE | Kubernetes (SUNK, CKS) | Managed API Gateway |
| Networking Fabric | Standard Ethernet | InfiniBand (Quantum-2) | Custom ASIC Interconnect |
| Context Window Limits | High (User Configured) | Maximum (Custom VRAM Tuning) | Model-Specific (Fixed) |
| Best Use Case | Legacy App Integration | Custom Model Fine-Tuning | Ultra-Fast Agentic Loops |

At the base of the stack is the physical hardware layer. For your custom model hosting, we recommend deploying on neoclouds that offer NVIDIA H200 or B200 instances. The H200 is a significant upgrade over the older H100, offering 141GB of HBM3e memory and 4.8 terabytes per second of memory bandwidth. This extra memory allows you to fit larger models on a single GPU, reducing the need for complex, slow multi-GPU tensor parallelism.

...

First, let us look at the real costs. Bare-metal GPU clouds are not designed for cheap, casual development. CoreWeave, for instance, does not sell single-GPU H100 instances on-demand. They sell exclusively in 8-GPU HGX bundles, which start at $49.24 per hour. This means your minimum commitment to spin up a single production node is $1,181 per day, or roughly $35,450 per month, even if your server sits completely idle for half the day. While providers like Lambda Labs offer single-GPU options starting at $3.99 per hour for H100 PCIe instances, capacity is highly constrained and frequently sold out.

...

What is the minimum cost to run on CoreWeave?

CoreWeave primarily sells accelerated compute through committed, multi-year contracts or on-demand 8-GPU HGX nodes. The on-demand rate for an 8-GPU H100 node is $49.24 per hour, which equates to roughly $35,450 per month. There are generally no single-GPU on-demand options on CoreWeave, making it an enterprise-focused platform.

results.title: CME Group plánuje futures navázané na ceny pronájmu čipů Nvidia
highlights:
# CME Group plánuje futures navázané na ceny pronájmu čipů Nvidia

 29 srpna, 2026 2 min. čtení 

CME ​ Group plánuje 5. října spustit futures kontrakty navázané na hodinové ceny pronájmu grafických procesorů Nvidia ​ H100 a B200. Zahájení obchodování podléhá regulatornímu schválení. Kontrakty se budou vypořádávat podle benchmarků společnosti Silicon Data, která sleduje ceny placené za pronájem těchto čipů.

Benchmark pro H100 nyní činí přibližně 2,68 USD za GPU-hodinu, zatímco u novějšího B200 dosahuje zhruba 5,66 USD. Obě hodnoty se během posledního roku výrazně měnily, přičemž jejich vývoj nebyl vždy shodný. Cenu výpočetního výkonu kromě typu čipu ovlivňují také poskytovatel, lokalita, délka pronájmu, síťové parametry a dostupnost.

Futures nebudou zajišťovat fyzickou rezervaci čipů, ale pouze finanční vypořádání podle změny benchmarkové ceny. Nvidia mezitím pro fiskální rok 2028 předpovídá přibližně 70% růst tržeb, a to navzdory omezené nabídce. Historické pokusy vytvořit obdobné trhy, například futures na čipy DRAM, počasí či síťovou kapacitu, měly smíšené výsledky kvůli obtížné standardizaci podkladových aktiv.
